doc.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998

title: Early trumpet teachers: the Hartleys and Fred Griffin
summary: Wilder studied briefly with Cliff Hartley and then with cornet soloist Fred Griffin, a stickler for sound who had also taught his father and played on local radio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: You know I studied with a teacher, I had a very fine teacher and everything. I had a couple of teachers prior to him, they were friends of my father’s, and one, what was his © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

name, Chauncy Welsh was a saxophone player with Cab Calloway’s band — not Chauncy Welsh, Chauncy Hartley. And he had a brother, Cliff Hartley, who was a very good trumpet player. And he lived in Baltimore but he used to come to Philadelphia. And I studied with him for a while, only a short time. And then my father decided that I should study with a man named Fred Griffin, who was a cornet soloist. He played these same kinds of solos as Del Staigers and Herbert Clarke and these people. And I studied with him. And he was a stickler for sound on the instrument, that you had to get a big sound on the instrument. He stressed that and technique. And he had taught my father. My father played sousaphone, he played cornet in the beginning, and he studied with Mr. Griffin, and then he switched to sousaphone and Griffin taught piano, trumpet, trombone and almost all the brass instruments. And so I studied with him, and he was one of these teachers that when you’d play out of the Arban book we were using, and he knew this thing inside out. And he’d say and he’d tell you what exercise to play, and you’d play it, and he’d say “that’s not a C, that was an E flat” or something. That’s what the note is. And he’d literally beat it into me. But that’s where it comes from.
You got some discipline out of that I would imagine.

He was a tremendous player though, because at one of the radio stations, I think it was WPEN or WCAU, I’m not sure which it was, but at any rate, they would have a period during which they had no scheduling of any commercial thing or something, and they’d just have a time slot that they had nothing to fill it in with, and they would call him and there was a pianist named Franklin Haweksberry, and he was a concert pianist, and he would accompany Fred Griffin on these cornet solos, and the network would call and say we need you for an hour or a half hour to play cornet solos to fill in the spot, and that’s what he did. He was a really fine player.
That’s interesting. Those days are pretty much gone of someone coming in and playing live for an hour.
